rationale: John 10:27 supports taking the Shepherd’s “voice” metonymically as what He says—His words or message—which the sheep hear and follow. The strongest alternative emphasizes Christ’s recognizable personal call, authority, and relationship with His sheep, but that is a broader account of the same communication rather than a contradictory referent. Nothing supplied shows that “voice” in this passage must exclude the Shepherd’s words. The entry is concise and nonexclusive, so the broader biblical uses of voice do not defeat it.
book_core_identification: “Voice” signifies the words or communicated speech of the speaker.
book_secondary_elaborations: In John 10:27, the Shepherd’s voice is His words.
chapter_only_objections: The chapter’s further identification of the stranger as anyone outside the covenant, and the stranger’s voice as the teaching of those outside it, goes beyond what the glossary entry asserts and is not established by John 10:27 alone.

John 10:3-5 may emphasize recognition of the shepherd’s identity and relationship with the sheep as well as recognition of propositional teaching; the chapter’s fuller application should not erase that emphasis.
strongest_counter_interpretation: In John 10, the Shepherd’s voice symbolizes Christ’s recognizable personal summons and authoritative communication, emphasizing the sheep’s relationship with and recognition of Him rather than identifying voice narrowly with semantic words.
counter_core_identification: The Shepherd’s voice is His recognizable, authoritative personal communication or call.
material_core_denial: The counter does not materially deny the book’s core: a speaker’s words are a principal form of the personal communication or call described by the counter.
counter_case: John 10:3-5 stresses that the sheep know the shepherd’s voice and distinguish it from strangers, which naturally highlights recognition of the speaker.
The wider biblical voice motif can emphasize presence, authority, sound, summons, or power rather than words alone.
John 10:27 itself says “voice,” not explicitly “words” or “teaching.”
book_explanatory_advantages: It gives a direct and economical account of what the sheep hear before they follow.
It fits the ordinary metonymy by which a speaker’s “voice” denotes the speaker’s utterance or message.
It coheres with the broader Christian interpretation of voice as authoritative communication while specifying the communicative content.
Its wording does not expressly deny relational recognition, authority, or other contextual emphases.
counter_explanatory_advantages: It more fully captures the recognition contrast between the shepherd and strangers in John 10:3-5.
It accommodates biblical passages where voice emphasizes identity, presence, power, or summons rather than propositional content.
decisive_sources: John 10:3-5 as quoted and discussed in the supporting chapter
unresolved_objections: The generic wording “the words of the one who speaks” should be understood as a symbolic or metonymic identification, not as an exhaustive lexical definition of every biblical occurrence of “voice.”
The single printed reference establishes the Shepherd application more clearly than it establishes a universal rule for all uses of “voice.”
